newsitem.title: USA: IFOR investigates Bosnian arms smuggling claim.
newsitem.headline: IFOR investigates Bosnian arms smuggling claim.

text.p: The NATO-led peace force in Bosnia is investigating reports that Bosnia's government is smuggling in heavy artillery, but neither it nor the United States has evidence of it, the State Department said Friday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns was commenting on a New York Times report that the Moslem-led government in Sarajevo had smuggled in 40 155-mm howitzers through the Adriatic port of Ploce in August, with assistance from Turkey and Malaysia.
The shipment of undeclared heavy weapons into Bosnia by any of the ethnic factions -- Moslems, Serbs or Croats -- would be a violation of the Dayton peace accord.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the IFOR peace force was investigating the allegations. But, he added, "neither IFOR nor the United States have any information that would back up these claims."
"Based on a preliminary set of discussions that we've had in the region today, we don't believe that there's been any large-scale smuggling of large-scale weaponry," he said.
But, he added, it would be rash to assert that there had been no smuggling of any sort.

Burns said the United States had been aware of the claims for several weeks. "They are serious charges, so IFOR is looking into them, and I think we will be very interested in seeing the results of that investigation," he said.

The New York Times, quoting a senior NATO official, said the howitzers had been smuggled through Ploce, in Croatia, to the Moslem-controlled town of Zenica in Bosnia in containers belonging to Turkish and Malaysian IFOR troops.
The Bosnian government can legally import heavy weapons up to a ceiling specified by Dayton. If it imports arms above that level, older weapons must be destroyed.
"Should there be a violation, that would be a very serious matter. And we'd certainly take it up at the highest level," Burns told a news briefing.

The United States is supplying Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation with $100 million of arms in an attempt to make it a match for the Bosnian Serbs. But it is delaying delivery until Sarajevo fires Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic, whom Washington considers too close to Iran.

Burns said Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum would set off for the Balkans Saturday for talks with Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian officials on their cooperation with the Hague-based Yugoslav war crimes tribunal.
